clue.text: Information hiding up in caves a bat adopted

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means read from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
something hiding sits concealed inside something else, so the letters lie inside a run of clue words

parts.note: the run of letters sitting across these words, read as printed

explanation.surface: A report on a colony of bats that has made its home deep in some caves.
explanation.walkthrough: Read cavES A BAT ADopted backwards and DATABASE appears; the answer is split across the two linked lights 1 and 2.
explanation.definitionFit: A database is an organised store of facts and records, so the word stands for stored information.

clue.text: See 1
Stock gift containing lead free pen

indicators.note: free of its lead means without its leading letter, so the front letter is dropped
to contain is to hold within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a boon is a blessing or gift
a quill is an old writing pen; without its first letter it leaves these four

explanation.surface: A shareholder receives a present of a pen that uses no lead in its ink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead free pen' reads like an eco-friendly writing instrument; it is QUILL losing its lead letter, which then sits inside BOON.
explanation.definitionFit: Bouillon is the French word for a clear broth, which is the liquid cooks call stock.

clue.text: Two cups overturned following half Arabic source of fizz

indicators.note: taking half of a word keeps one equal portion of its letters and discards the rest

parts.note: the second half of the six letters

indicators.note: something overturned is flipped upside down, so in a down entry its letters run the other way

parts.note: a bra has two cups

explanation.surface: Coffee cups knocked over in a café, with half the Arabic coffee lost as it fizzes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two cups' is a bra, a crossword favourite; turned over it sits after the back half of ARABIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Bicarb, short for bicarbonate of soda, releases carbon dioxide bubbles, so it is the thing that makes drinks and powders fizz.

clue.text: Cycle fork in a squat leads to court trouble

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it
to cycle is to go round, so the last letter comes round to the front

parts.note: taken as written
to squat is to sit on one's haunches
taken as written before being cycled

explanation.surface: A broken bicycle fork left in a squat ends up with someone being taken to court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle fork' reads as a bike part, but 'cycle' is an instruction: the last letter rotates round to the front before the result goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To court trouble is to invite it by reckless behaviour, which is exactly what the idiom about provoking consequences means.

clue.text: After singer departs for church

indicators.note: X for Y means X put in place of Y, so one piece takes over another's slot

parts.note: Beyoncé, the American pop star
D is the abbreviation for departs on timetables
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Once the singer has left, everyone heads off to church.
explanation.walkthrough: The final CE of BEYONCE is swapped for D. 'Departs' looks like a verb about the singer leaving; it is the timetable abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Beyond can mean later than a point in time, as in 'beyond midnight', matching a preposition meaning later.

clue.text: Carry On Doctor, in one cut

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or falsify, so the letters are altered into a new order

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The 1967 comedy film Carry On Doctor, released in a single uncut version.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic title Carry On Doctor hides both the definition and the anagram signal; Carry On films were a long-running series of British comedy movies.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry on is to keep going without stopping, the ordinary meaning of the verb to persist.

clue.text: A European railway's cheating

parts.note: A was the British film certificate for adult viewing
E is the standard abbreviation for European
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A continental train company has been caught fiddling its accounts or its tickets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' looks like the article, but it expands to ADULT, from the old British A film certificate.
explanation.definitionFit: Adultery is being unfaithful to a spouse, which in everyday speech is called cheating on a partner.

clue.text: No Deal act, Boris and I worked up — it helped Johnson win once

indicators.note: worked up means agitated or stirred, so the letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: the letters of the first part of the fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: Brexit politics: a No Deal act, with Boris Johnson and the speaker getting agitated over it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at Boris Johnson; the definition's Johnson is Ben Johnson, the sprinter stripped of his 1988 Olympic 100m gold after testing positive for steroids.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Johnson won the 1988 Olympic sprint while using a performance-enhancing drug of this class, later disqualified for it.

clue.text: Country accepted organised crime ace

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for accepted

indicators.note: to organise is to arrange, so these letters are put into a new arrangement

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
A is ace on a playing card

explanation.surface: A nation has come to accept organised crime as something it excels at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organised crime' reads as one phrase, the Mafia; split it, and 'organised' is the signal to rearrange CRIME.
explanation.definitionFit: America is commonly used as the name of the United States, a nation state.

clue.text: Saw a team keeping two metres apart

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds the other
things held apart are separated, with something placed between them

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for metre, twice
taken as written
a team of eleven, as in cricket or football, is an XI

explanation.surface: A team spotted keeping two metres apart, as under social-distancing rules.
explanation.walkthrough: The two Ms are the 'apart' ones, holding A XI between them. 'Saw' looks like a past tense verb but is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying or proverb, and a maxim is a short statement of a general truth.

clue.text: Regularly ignored forlorn St Paul's altar hanging

indicators.note: ignoring at a regular interval skips every other letter, keeping the rest

parts.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A neglected, sorry-looking hanging on the altar of St Paul's Cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the odd letters of FoRlOrN sT pAuLs spells the answer; St Paul's is London's cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: A frontal is a decorated cloth panel covering the front of a church altar.

clue.text: Old character voiced legendary blade

indicators.note: something voiced is spoken, so the result is judged by its sound

parts.note: old gives ex, as in former, and character gives calibre, meaning quality

explanation.surface: An old character actor provided the voice of a mythical warrior's sword.
explanation.walkthrough: EX (old) plus CALIBRE (character) spoken together sound like the sword's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Excalibur is King Arthur's sword in the Arthurian legends, drawn from the stone or given by the Lady of the Lake.

clue.text: Social distance one street away

indicators.note: whatever is away is gone, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Social distancing: stay a street's length away from anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social distance' reads as one pandemic phrase; 'Social' alone is the definition, a noun meaning a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A social is an informal party or gathering, and a dance is exactly such an evening event.

clue.text: Influence Independent politician in General Election initially

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for Independent
an MP is a Member of Parliament
taken as written

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: How much sway can an independent candidate have at a general election?
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal but is simply part of the string.
explanation.definitionFit: To impinge on something is to have an effect on it, so the verb works as a synonym for influence.

clue.text: Formality over college paper — it's a sweet course

parts.note: ice is cold reserve or stiffness of manner
C is the abbreviation for college
a ream is 500 sheets of paper

explanation.surface: The fuss about a university essay is described as an easy option for students.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' places the first piece above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice cream is served as a dessert, the sweet course at the end of a meal.

clue.text: Today Klopp is lacking finishers, but looking towards the top spot

indicators.note: lacking their finishers means the words lose their final letters
in a down entry, facing the top means reading from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: the word without its last letter
the name without its last letter

explanation.surface: Jürgen Klopp's Liverpool are missing strikers today yet still eyeing first place in the league.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top spot' looks like the definition, a league position; only 'spot' defines, and 'the top' belongs to the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A polka dot is one of the round dots in a regular pattern on fabric, so it is a spot.

clue.text: Turned up noise to conceal Military Intelligence — special release

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide within, so one piece goes inside the other
turned up in a down clue means flipped to read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written
MI is the standard abbreviation
S is the abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: A loud noise covers up a secret intelligence operation's special release of information.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up noise' reads as volume being raised; in a down clue it means the word read upwards, with the spy agency and special slipped in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An emission is something given off or discharged, the same sense as a release of gas or light.

clue.text: Attempt to take in old play

indicators.note: to take in is to admit inside, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: a try is an attempt
aged means old

explanation.surface: Someone tries to go and see a classic piece of theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take in' sounds like going to see a show; it is the signal for TRY to hold AGED.
explanation.definitionFit: A tragedy is a drama with a sorrowful ending, one kind of stage play.

clue.text: Obvious answer pages are not vacuous

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
pp is the abbreviation for pages
taken as written

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word loses its insides and keeps its two ends

parts.note: just the first and last letters

explanation.surface: The answer is plain to see: these pages are far from empty-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not vacuous' reads as meaning full or meaningful; 'vacuous' empties NOT down to its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparent means clearly visible or plain to understand, a direct synonym for evident.

clue.text: Lag finally escaped lock-up

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means reading from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: Yale is a well-known brand of lock

explanation.surface: An old convict has at last broken out of the prison where he was locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lag' is British slang for a convict, which drives the prison story; 'lock-up' is not a jail but a lock read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A lag is a gap in time between events, the same sense as a hold-up or wait.

clue.text: Naked pecs? Add muscle for striking effect

indicators.note: naked means stripped of coverings, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: the letters left inside
the lats are the latissimus dorsi back muscles

explanation.surface: A bodybuilder posing shirtless adds muscle definition for a more impressive look.
explanation.walkthrough: Stripping PECS to EC and adding LAT, a gym word for a back muscle, gives the French borrowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Éclat is brilliant show or dazzling success, a flourish that creates a strong impression.

clue.text: This number's dry without singer's introduction

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: thirsty means dry, in need of a drink

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A singer complains that this song feels flat without a proper introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a song; it is simply a number word. 'This' is loose, as the clue's own number is 22, not the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirty is a cardinal numeral, three times ten, so it is a number in the counting sense.

clue.text: Useless sailor emptied latrine after panic at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
AB is an able-bodied seaman

indicators.note: an emptied word has lost its contents, keeping only its two ends

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A hopeless deckhand cleans out the ship's toilet after everyone panics during a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the naval picture but is the anagram signal, and 'after' means the jumbled word comes first, before the sailor and the emptied toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Incapable means lacking the ability to do something, so a useless person is incapable.

clue.text: Inferior, firm rump

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
arse is British slang for backside

explanation.surface: A cut of meat described as a poor-quality, tough piece of rump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' reads as describing the rump's texture; it is a business, CO.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse means rough and of low quality, as in coarse cloth, so it matches second-rate.

clue.text: Stage crew run over crazy ideas

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: something crazy is disordered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The backstage team goes over some wild ideas before the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run over' looks like rehearsing; it is two cricket abbreviations, from scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: Roadies travel with touring bands, setting up and dismantling the equipment used in concerts.

clue.text: Master follows athletic sidekick to find Tardis, say

parts.note: A is an abbreviation for athletic, as in team names
a crony is a close companion
M is the abbreviation for master

explanation.surface: Doctor Who's arch-enemy the Master trails the Doctor's sporty companion to locate the time machine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Master, the companion and the Tardis all come from Doctor Who, the BBC science-fiction series; 'follows' puts M after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: TARDIS stands for Time And Relative Dimension In Space, a word formed from initial letters, so it is an example.

clue.text: Local girl's close shave

parts.note: local means close by
a young woman

explanation.surface: A young woman from the neighbourhood gets a very clean shave at the barber's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close shave' reads as barbering; it is the idiom for a narrow escape.
explanation.definitionFit: A close shave is an idiom for a narrow escape from disaster, the same thing as an accident that nearly happened.

clue.text: See 27
Famous host, Danny broadcast for ages

definitions.note: the answer is a noun phrase meaning a very long time; 'for' is folded into the idiom

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: the fifteen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A well-known presenter called Danny has been on the air for a very long time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the presenter picture but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means an extremely long time, as in 'not in a month of Sundays', the same as ages.
